## Estimating effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$ using Sechenov relationship

The concentration of ions in soil solution affects not only the activity coefficients but also the solubility of $CO_2$ through Henry's law constant $pK_H$. Unfortunately, the mathematical expression of this effect is difficult to apply accurately in case of soil solution, because several different ions are typically present in there. The general relationship between $pK_H$ and concentration of ions in soil solution is defined by following equation:

$$pK_H = pK_{H,0} - \sum[h_i + h_{G,0} + h_T \times (T-298.15)] \times c_i $$ {#eq-63}

in which $pK_{H,0}$ is Henry's law constant for pure water (@eq-18), $pK_H$ is the constant for a solution that contains several ions ($i$). Concentration of each ion in $mol \times L^{-1}$ is defined by variable $c_i$ and its effect on $pK_H$ is defined by a empirically estimated parameter $h_i$ in $L \times mol^{-1}$. Finally, variables $h_{G,0}$ (in $L \times mol^{-1}$) and $h_T$ (in $L \times mol^{-1} \times K^{-1}$) are two gas specific (i.e. $CO_2$ specific in this case) variables, again experimentally derived. The first applies to standard temperature 298.15 K, and the second defines the temperature sensitivity. Every gas has its own $h_{G,0}$ and $h_T$, and every ion present in soil solution has its own $h_i$. @eq-63 cannot be applied if concentrations of all ions in soil solution are not known. This is the reason for why the @eq-63 is so difficult to use. Concentrations of all ions in soil solution is rarely known and that limits the use of eq. 63 @eq-63. We will use the data of @stednick1984 reported above to quantify the effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$.

According to Weisenberger and Schumpe  -@weisenberger1996, $CO_2$ specific variables $h_{G,0}$ and $h_T$ are respectively $-0.0172~L \times mol^{-1}$ and $-0.338 \times 10^{-3}~L \times mol^{-1}$. At 20°C (293.15 K), $-0.0172 - 0.338 \times 10^{-3} \times (293.15 - 298.15) = -0.01551$ is added to all $h_i$ of all ions in soil solution. Values of $h_i$ of each ion measured by Stednick -@stednick1984 in soil solution are reported in the table below.

| Ion | $h_i$ in $L \times mol^{-1}$ | Concentrations in $\mu mol \times L^{-1}$ |
|:----------------:|:----------------:|:----------------------------------:|
| $H^+$ | 0 | 1.6 |
| $K^+$ | 0.0922 | 15 |
| $Ca^{+2}$ | 0.1762 | 40 |
| $Mg^{+2}$ | 0.1694 | 23.5 |
| $Na^+$ | 0.1143 | 96 |
| $Fe^{+2}$ | 0.1523 | 0.3 |
| $SO_4^{-2}$ | 0.1172 | 130 |
| $Cl^-$ | 0.0318 | 273 |

According to @eq-18, $pK_{H,0}$ is -1.41 at 20°C. Applying @eq-63, $pK_H$ is expected to be:

$$\displaylines{
pK_H = -1.41 - [(0 -0.01551) \times 1.6 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{17mm} (H^+)\\
     \hspace{20mm} + (0.0922 -0.01551) \times 15 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (K^+) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1762 -0.01551) \times 40 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Ca^{+2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1694 -0.01551) \times 23.5 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Mg^{+2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1143 -0.01551) \times 96 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Na^{+}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1523 -0.01551) \times 0.3 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Fe^{+2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1172 -0.01551) \times 130 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (SO_4^{-2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.0318 -0.01551) \times 273 \times 10^{-6} \hspace{20mm} (Cl^{-}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} = -1.41 - 5.52 \times 10^{-5} \approx -1.41 \hspace{20mm}
   }$$ {#eq-64}

The effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$ is negligible in this case. @eq-63 is typically used to calculate $CO_2$ solubility in sea water with nearly molar concentrations of $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$. The effect of soil solution chemistry on $pK_H$ can be neglected in many soils. However, in very saline soils this effect becomes significant. Let's document it on an example.

In the following example, we will use @eq-63 to calculate $pK_H$ of $CO_2$ for dry steppe solonetz using measured ion concentrations reported in Endovitsky et al. -@endovitsky2014. The ion concentrations are reported in a table below:

| Ion | $h_i$ in $L \times mol^{-1}$ | Concentrations in $mmol \times L^{-1}$ |
|:----------------:|:----------------:|:----------------------------------:|
| $HCO_3^-$ | 0.0967 | 8.88 |
| $CO_3^{-2}$ | 0.1423 | 0.72 |
| $Ca^{+2}$ | 0.1762 | 9.73 |
| $Mg^{+2}$ | 0.1694 | 77.5 |
| $Na^+$ | 0.1143 | 270.4 |
| $SO_4^{-2}$ | 0.1172 | 137.2 |
| $Cl^-$ | 0.0318 | 160.2 |

According to reported soil solution composition, $pK_H$ at 20°C is expected to be:

$$\displaylines{
pK_H = -1.41 - [(0.0967 -0.01551) \times 8.88 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{17mm} (HCO_3^-)\\
     \hspace{20mm} + (0.1423 -0.01551) \times 0.72 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (CO_3^{-2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1762 -0.01551) \times 9.73 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Ca^{+2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1694 -0.01551) \times 77.5 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Mg^{+2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1143 -0.01551) \times 270.4 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Na^{+}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.1172 -0.01551) \times 137.2 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (SO_4^{-2}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} + (0.0318 -0.01551) \times 160.2 \times 10^{-3} \hspace{20mm} (Cl^{-}) \\
   \hspace{20mm} = -1.41 - 0.0576 = -1.468 \hspace{20mm} 
   }$$ {#eq-65}

As compared to $pK_{H,0}$, $pK_H$ is lower so the $CO_2$ solubility decreases in this saline soil by $(1 - 10^{-1.468 + 1.41}) \times 100 = 12.5 \%$. Nevertheless, the salinity also affects the dissociation due to high ionic strength of the solution. Let's compare decrease in solubility with the effect of high ionic strength on the dissociation. To perform the comparison, we need to calculate ionic strength of soil solution using @eq-49:

$$\displaylines{
I = \frac{1 \times 10^{-3}}{2} \times (8.88 \times 1^2 [HCO_3^{-}] + 0.72 \times 2^2 [CO_3^{-2}] + 9.73 \times 2^2 [Ca^{+2}] \\
   \hspace{20mm} +  77.5 \times 2^2[Mg^{+2}] + 270.4 \times 1^2 [Na^+] + 137.4 \times 2^2 [SO_4^{-2}] + 16.2 \times 1^2 [Cl^-]) \\
   \hspace{80mm}= 0.6~mol \times L 
}$$ {#eq-66}

Knowing the ionic strength, we can further calculate activity coefficients $\gamma_{HCO_3^-}$, $\gamma_{CO_3^{-2}}$ and $\gamma_{H^+}$ using @eq-51 - -@eq-53:

$$\gamma_{HCO_3^-} = 10^{- \frac{0.507 \times 1^2 \times \sqrt 0.6}{1 + 0.3282 \times 5.4 \times \sqrt 0.6}} = 0.68 $$ {#eq-67}

$$\gamma_{CO_3^{-2}} = 10^{- \frac{0.507 \times 2^2 \times \sqrt 0.6}{1 + 0.3282 \times 5.4 \times \sqrt0.6}} = 0.22 $$ {#eq-68}

$$\gamma_{H^{+}} = 10^{- \frac{0.507 \times 1^2 \times \sqrt 0.6}{1 + 0.3282 \times 9 \times \sqrt 0.6}} = 0.76 $$ {#eq-68}

Finally, we can quantify the relative change in the amount of IC in soil solution with a composition reported above and pH of 8.85 as compared to pure water using an equation:

$$\displaylines{
\Delta IC [\%] =(\frac{10^{pK_H} + 10^{pK_H + pK_1 + pH - log(\gamma_{H^+}) - log(\gamma_{HCO_3^-})} + 10^{pK_H + pK_1 + pK_2 + 2\times pH - 2 \times log(\gamma_{H^+}) - log(\gamma_{CO_3^{-2}})}}{10^{pK_{H, 0}} + 10^{pK_{H, 0} + pK_1 + pH} + 10^{pK_{H, 0} + pK_1 + pK_2 + 2\times pH}} - 1) \times 100 \\
   \hspace{80mm}= 84 \%
}$$ {#eq-70}

The effect of ionic strength on total IC in soil solution through its effect on activity coefficients is greater than the effect of soil solution composition through its effect on $pK_H$. Even though the high concentration of ions in soil solution reduces solubility of $CO_2$, it increases the magnitude of dissociation. Neglecting the effect of composition of soil solution will cause an underestimation of total IC rather than overestimation. On the other hand, if we decide to correct our calculations for ionic strength effect only because it is easier to calculate, our results will be overestimated by approx. 30%. Due to such complexity, it is recommended not to use gas chromatography when respiration rate is measured in highly saline soils. Instead, older and, unfortunately, more tedious method of soil incubation with cup containing strong alkali is recommended.
